title: 📊 2024 Oscar Prediction Challenge
text:
📊 2024 Oscar Prediction Challenge
This interactive Shiny app presents the results of a survey where participants predicted the winners of various Oscar categories. Built as part of my efforts to create and share data-driven projects, the dashboard lets users explore trends, accuracy, and insights from the challenge.




📊 COvid-19 Dashboard
The Covid-19 Dashboard is an interactive tool analyzing cases and fatalities in both the United States and my home state of Oregon. Originally created as a class project at the start of the pandemic, it has gone through multiple iterations to become a fully functional and informative resource for exploring trends over time.

title: About Me
text:
I was born, raised, and currently reside in the City of Roses—Portland, Oregon. I have a passion for making data meaningful, accessible, and equitable. I believe in continuously improving how we work with data—whether that’s through better governance, building tools, or supporting making informed data driven decisions. My portfolio is a collection of data visuals, blogs, and dashboards mostly built in R.
I currently work in state government, where I lead data efforts to improve reporting, governance, and innovation at Paid Leave Oregon. I also collaborate with data analysts and engineers across agencies to build better data systems and insights.
The best way to reach me professionally is through LinkedIn—just send me a message. Email also works, but since my inbox is over a decade old, messages sometimes get lost in the noise.

title: About
text:
💚 What I Do ~
I currently work in state government, where I lead data efforts to improve reporting, governance, and innovation at Paid Leave Oregon. I also collaborate with data analysts and engineers across agencies to build better data systems and insights. Outside of work, I’m active in the PDX R User Group, where I’ve given a lightning talk and stay connected with the local R community.

title: About
text:
💚 Where I Came From ~
I have a BS in Mathematics from Portland State University, where I studied statistics and first learned R. Before working in government, I worked in fintech and digital advertising. Earlier in my career, I held a variety of roles—accounting at a sheet metal company, admin / safety monitoring for a roofing business, and even managing shifts at Baskin-Robbins and a dispensary.
My background isn’t just in data—I was also a trained dancer, studying pre-professionally at the San Francisco Conservatory of Ballet. Some of my biggest role models were my dance teachers, who taught me the value of instinct, adaptability, and looking at movement (or data) from multiple perspectives.
When I was 21, I was in a head-on collision with a drunk driver, led to multiple jaw surgeries and a long recovery. That experience shaped my views on workplace support and the necessity of programs like paid leave. No one should have to struggle through major life events without the ability to take time off.

Applied mapping and data analytics techniques to investigate dispensary diversity in Oregon November 2020 where I discovered that more than half of dispensaries in Oregon are owned by chains, and about 10% of dispensaries in Portland’s Urban Growth Boundary are owned by one chain, Groundworks.

title: Text Mining, Sentiment Analysis, & Topic Modeling
text: These notes provide a quick reference for key concepts in text mining, sentiment analysis, and topic modeling, including considerations for choosing and interpreting a topic model.

title: Text Mining, Topic Modeling, & Sentiment Analysis
text: Word (\(\text{w}\))

title: Text Mining, Topic Modeling, & Sentiment Analysis
text: Word (\(w\))

title: Text Mining, Sentiment Analysis, & Topic Modeling
text:
Definitions
(\(w\)) Word: a single word. This is the smallest unit of analysis.
Text: written content (aka the words) within a single document.
(\(d\)) Document: a unit of text.
Corpus: the full collection of texts (documents).
Stop Words: common words that don’t add much meaning for text analysis.
(\(y\)) Covariates: document attributes.
(\(v\)) Vocabulary: a unique set of words from a corpus.
N-Grams: sequence of words we can use to look for corpus themes such as uni-gram (one word), bi-gram (two words), and tri-gram (three words).
Sentiment: emotional tone or attitude expressed in the text.

title: Text Mining, Sentiment Analysis, & Topic Modeling
text:
Definitions
Topics: groups of words that tend to appear together and represent possible themes.
(\(k\)) Number of Topics: the number of themes your model should look for, where each topic is a probability distribution over the words. Higher K can capture more nuance but risks redundancy and noise.
Exclusivity: is how unique a topic’s top words are to that topic. Higher exclusivity means the words are more distinct, but topics can also get more fragmented. This often trades off with coherence.
Semantic Coherence: measures how often a topic’s top words occur together in documents, helping assess whether the words in that topic are related. This tends to decrease as \(k\) grows and topics get thinner.
Held-Out: predicts the fit on held out words or unseen data. Higher is better, and you want to look for when K levels out (the elbow).
Residuals: this shows the unexplained variance, and is the difference between predicted and actual values. High residuals suggests missing topics or vocabulary issues. This usually drops fast with K, and then should flatten out.

title: Text Mining, Sentiment Analysis, & Topic Modeling
text:
Considerations
When choosing \(k\), the main things to consider are:

Where does held-out mostly plateau?
Where do residuals start to flatten out?
Where are exclusivity and coherence both reasonable?

title: Text Mining, Sentiment Analysis, & Topic Modeling
text:
Definitions

(\(\beta\)) Distribution of Words in a Topic
The vocabulary (mix of words) that defines a topic.
(How likely a word occurs in a topic.)
\[\beta_{d,k}=P(w_v|k,y_d)\]
The word distribution for topic \(k\) is the probability of vocabulary word \(w_v\), given topic \(k\) and the document-level covariates \(y_d\).


(\(z_{d,n}\)) Topic Assignment (per word)
The topic assigned to a specific word in a specific document.
(Which topic generated a specific word.)
\[z_{d,n} \in \{1, \ldots, K\}\]
For the \(n\)th word in document \(d\), which topic \(k\) generated that word.


(\(\theta\)) Distribution of Topics in a Document
The mix of topics a document covers.
(Document d is 70% topic 1 and 30% topic 2. )
\[\theta_{d,k} = P(z = k \mid d)\]
For document \(d\), \(\theta_{d,k}\) is the probability that a word in that document belongs to topic \(k\).


(\(y_d\)) Covariate Effect
Document-level attributes, such as a response date or group, that can help explain differences in how common topics are across documents, the words used to express a topic, or both.


Latent Variables
Hidden variables that are a part of the model that we do not directly observe, but want to infer.

title: How I Use AI
text:
I use AI as a tool to support my personal projects and explore new ideas. Depending on the project, I may use it to brainstorm, work through questions, refine writing, or help develop and troubleshoot code.
For this website, I have used AI to help update the design and code. I guide the process, make decisions about what to include, and review the results.
My use of AI varies from project to project. When it plays a significant role in a post or project, I may include additional details about how I used it.

title: R and SQLite
text: This post compares R and SQL approaches to the same data questions. It is for anyone learning either language or interested in seeing how familiar data tasks translate between them.

title: R and SQLite
text:
Packages
For all my data queries and manipulation in R I will be using base R, dplyr, and magrittr.

library(dplyr)
library(magrittr)

To create a SQL database, and run SQL queries in R chunks I will be using a package called RSQLite.

# install.packages("RSQLite")
library(RSQLite)

Warning: package 'RSQLite' was built under R version 4.5.2

title: R and SQLite
text:
Data
Data source: These examples use practice data from SQL Practice. The patient table contains a subset of 1,000 records used for this post.
The examples use three data sets:

patients: Which includes patient_id, first_name, last_name, gender, birth_date, city, province_id, allergies, height, and weight.


patients <- utils::read.csv('data/patients.csv')


province_names: Which includes province_id, and province_name.


province_names <- utils::read.csv("data/province_names.csv")


admissions: which includes patient_id, admission_date, discharge_date, diagnosis, attending_doctor_id


admissions <- utils::read.csv("data/admissions.csv")

title: R and SQLite
text:
Database
Create an in-memory SQLite database with dbConnect() and SQLite(). It exists for this R session and does not change a database file.

hosp <- RSQLite::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(),
                           ":memory:")

Use dbWriteTable() to add each data frame as a table in the database.

RSQLite::dbWriteTable(hosp,
                      "patients",
                      patients)
RSQLite::dbWriteTable(hosp,
                      "province_names",
                      province_names)
RSQLite::dbWriteTable(hosp,
                      "admissions",
                      admissions)

Verify the three data sets are in the database using:

dbListTables() to list the tables within the hosp database.


RSQLite::dbListTables(hosp)

[1] "admissions"     "patients"       "province_names"
